screens.title: Applying Firewall Filters
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll learn how firewall filters become active only after they are applied, how the application point and direction determine which packets are inspected, and why the loopback interface is the canonical place for control plane protection. You will see concrete examples of input and output filters, the impact of chaining filters, the specific role of lo0 when protecting the router's C P U, and the typical verification commands to confirm behavior. This matters because a misapplied filter can drop legitimate management traffic, lock you out of a device, or fail to stop an attack. For example, allowing SSH only from a management subnet and applying that filter to lo0 lets you restrict who can reach the router itself regardless of the ingress interface. We'll also cover the order of operations — input filter, uRPF checks, routing lookup, then output filter — so you understand when filters drop or allow packets relative to routing decisions. By the end of the lesson you will be able to apply filters to logical interfaces, create a control plane protection policy for lo0, and use Junos verification commands safely. Consider what access you need to preserve before you apply a restrictive filter; that habit prevents accidental lockouts.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Applying Firewall Filters
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Applying Firewall Filters

Understand input vs output, control plane protection on lo0, chaining, and verification commands.

Duration: ~15 minutes content
Why this chapter matters

A correctly applied filter prevents unwanted traffic from reaching internal networks or the router CPU. Misplaced filters can drop management access or miss traffic if applied on the wrong interface.

In this lesson

Apply filters to logical interfaces and choose input or output to control packet inspection timing.

Coming up

Protect lo0 for control plane protection and verify with counters and traffic monitoring.

Concept Map
Input vs Output → Chaining → lo0 CPP → Verification Commands
Logical interface & family
Control plane protection
Explore Key Topics
Input & Output
When a packet is inspected and how that affects routing and control plane reachability.
Control Plane Protection
Applying strict input filters on lo0 to protect the router's CPU and management plane.
Verification
Use counters, traffic monitor, and logs to confirm which terms match and what is discarded.
Key Takeaway

Attach filters deliberately and verify with counters and captures. For control plane protection, prefer lo0 input filters to centralize CPU protection.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply firewall filters to both physical and logical interfaces in Junos OS, choose the correct direction for filtering, and protect the control plane by applying a filter to lo0. You will learn how filters interact with routing and uRPF checks so you can predict when a packet will be accepted or discarded. You will also practice verification and troubleshooting workflows: checking which filters are applied, reading term counters, capturing traffic on an interface, and reviewing logs when log actions are configured. These are practical, testable skills: for example, you will apply an input filter to lo0 that only accepts SSH from a management subnet and then verify hits with show firewall filter counter. You will also be prepared to avoid common mistakes, like applying a restrictive filter to an in-band management interface without a console fallback. Together these objectives give you the procedural and diagnostic skills to apply filters safely and confirm they behave as intended in production.

Applied skills and safe practices

Practice creating filters that permit known management and protocol traffic and log or discard other traffic.

Skill
Compose accept terms

Define terms for SSH, BGP peers, and OSPF as needed and place a discard term last for unmatched traffic.

Skill
Chain filters safely

Skill
Verify matches and logs

Safety note

When applying filters to lo0 or management interfaces, keep a console or out-of-band connection available in case you lock yourself out.

screens.title: Applying a filter makes it active
screens.narratorSegment: A firewall filter in Junos only becomes active when it is applied to an interface and the appropriate family. Defining terms and actions inside the filter does nothing until you bind that filter to a logical unit such as unit 0 and to a family like inet for IPv4. This specificity matters because the same physical interface can support multiple families and logical units; a filter applied to family inet on unit 0 will not affect other families or units. For example, applying a filter to ge-0/0/0.0 family inet ensures IPv4 packets entering or leaving that logical interface are evaluated. A common misconception is assuming a filter defined under firewall will automatically protect interfaces globally — it will not. You must attach the filter to the interface using syntax such as filter input FILTER_NAME under interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet. When you attach a filter, decide whether it should inspect input traffic, output traffic, or both. Attaching to lo0 centralizes protection for packets destined to the router itself. Always verify attachment after commit with show interfaces detail to confirm the filter is present and in the expected direction. The key takeaway is: definition creates capability; attachment makes it operate.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Applying a filter makes it active
Concept

A filter must be attached to interfaces and a family to inspect packets. Logical units and family context determine which traffic is affected.

Example attachment
interfaces {
    ge-0/0/0 {
        unit 0 {
            family inet {
                filter {
                    input EXAMPLE_FILTER;
                }
                address 192.0.2.1/24;
            }
        }
    }
}
Explanation & checklist
  • Define the filter under firewall family inet filter NAME.
  • Attach using filter input|output FILTER_NAME under the interface family.
  • Confirm family matches the traffic type (inet for IPv4).
  • Use show interfaces <interface> detail to verify attachment.
Key Takeaway

Attachment is the activation step. Always verify that the correct family and unit were used when you apply a filter.

screens.title: Input filters
screens.narratorSegment: An input filter is applied to packets as they enter the router through a specific interface and is the most common place to enforce security policy. Because input filters are processed before routing lookup, they can stop unwanted traffic from consuming router resources or reaching internal networks. For instance, blocking a malicious SYN flood at the ingress input prevents the router from having to examine or forward those packets. Input filters work at the logical interface and family level — if you want to protect IPv4 arriving on ge-0/0/1, bind a filter under unit 0 family inet and use filter input FILTER_NAME. A common misconception is that an input filter on a single physical interface protects traffic destined to all of the router's IP addresses; it only affects packets arriving on that interface. To centrally protect the router itself, apply a control plane protection filter to lo0. Remember also that input filters are evaluated before unicast reverse path forwarding and routing lookup, so they can drop packets regardless of routing state. A practical check after applying an input filter is to use show firewall filter counter and monitor traffic on the interface to confirm the expected terms are being hit. What packet types will you prioritize in your input policy?

keyIdea.title: Input = early defense
keyIdea.text: Input filters evaluate packets as they arrive, before routing, so they are the first line of defense.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Input filters
What an input filter does

Input filters run on packets entering an interface and are processed before routing decisions are made.

Common use cases
  • Block malicious traffic before it reaches internal hosts.
  • Prevent resource exhaustion on the router by dropping undesired packets early.
  • Filter IPv4 or other families selectively on logical units.
Verification
Use show firewall filter <name> counter and monitor traffic on the ingress interface to confirm matching behavior.
Example scenario

You need to prevent unwanted IPv4 connections from reaching an internal network. Apply an input filter on the external-facing logical unit so those packets are evaluated and dropped before routing.

Common misconception

An input filter on one physical interface does not automatically protect all destinations on the router; it only affects packets arriving on that interface.

Key Takeaway

Use input filters to stop threats early, then verify with counters and traffic monitoring to ensure your terms match expected packets.

screens.title: Output filters
screens.narratorSegment: Output filters evaluate packets as they are about to leave an egress interface, after the routing lookup has determined the next hop and egress. Use output filters when you want to control traffic the router sends to a network segment or when you must enforce policy on egress behavior. For example, if you want to prevent the router from sending specific types of traffic to an internal network, applying an output filter on the internal-facing interface ensures those packets are checked after routing. A contrast often confuses students: input filters protect the ingress and can drop packets before the router spends C P U on routing; output filters do not prevent a packet from being routed internally and are applied later in the packet's journey. Another common use is to provide a last layer of defense in a layered policy approach — for instance, accept or rate-limit on ingress, then drop anything undesired before it exits the internal interface. Remember that output filters cannot protect the router's C P U from packets destined for the router itself; for that, use lo0 input filters. Verify output filters the same way with show interfaces detail and show firewall filter counters for the named filter applied outbound, and consider packet captures to confirm filtering behavior.

keyIdea.title: Output = final check
keyIdea.text: Output filters are applied after routing lookup and control what the router sends out on an egress interface.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Output filters
When to use output filters

Apply output filters when you need to control traffic leaving the router, or apply an egress policy after routing decisions are made.

Practical examples
  • Block specific TCP flows from being sent to an internal network.
  • Control egress traffic types after routing lookup completes.
Contrast with input filters

Input filters run before routing and can prevent resource usage. Output filters run after routing and act as a final check on packets about to leave.

Layered approach

Combine ingress and egress filters when you need layered defense: stop threats early and enforce egress policies later.

Verification

After applying an output filter, use show interfaces <name> detail and show firewall filter <name> counter to observe hits, and use monitor traffic on the egress interface if needed.

screens.title: Chaining filters and evaluation order
screens.narratorSegment: Junos lets you apply multiple filters in a chain for the same interface and direction, for example input [ FILTER_A FILTER_B ]. When chaining, filters are evaluated in sequence. The first filter that returns a terminating action — accept, discard, or reject — stops further processing. This sequential behavior is important when you design layered policies. For instance, you might place a lightweight, high-performance filter first to drop obvious unwanted traffic, then a more complex filter second for deeper inspection. A common pitfall is placing a permissive accept term too early in the chain so later filters never get an opportunity to apply their tighter rules. Another detail to remember is implicit discard: if no explicit term matches, the packet is discarded by default. That means chained filters must explicitly accept traffic you want to permit or include a permissive final term. When you chain filters, test each filter individually first using counters to ensure it behaves as expected. Use show firewall filter counter for each filter and then apply the chain and re-check to confirm the first-terminating behavior matches your design. How could you order terms to minimize false positives while limiting C P U cost?

keyIdea.title: First-terminating action wins
keyIdea.text: In a chained list, the first filter to accept or discard a packet stops further evaluation; order matters.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Chaining filters and evaluation order
Sequential evaluation

When you attach multiple filters in a list, they're checked in order. A terminating match stops evaluation immediately.

Step 1
Filter A evaluated first
Step 2
If Filter A accepts or discards, stop
Step 3
Otherwise evaluate Filter B
Verification pattern

Check counters per filter before and after chaining to confirm which filter produced the terminating action.

Design tip

Place cheap rejects or fast checks early to reduce CPU cost, and reserve expensive matches for later filters only if earlier checks pass.

Pitfall

Avoid broad accept terms early in the chain that prevent later, more specific security checks from running.

screens.title: Control Plane Protection (CPP)
screens.narratorSegment: Control plane protection uses firewall filters to restrict traffic destined to the router itself — the C P U that processes management and routing protocol packets. The loopback interface, lo0, is the standard place to apply CPP filters because traffic destined to any of the router's IP addresses will ultimately be processed there if lo0 is configured with those addresses. By placing an input filter on lo0 that permits only specific management networks, routing neighbors, and protocol traffic, you centralize protection regardless of the physical interface on which a packet first arrived. For example, a PROTECT_LO0 filter might accept SSH from 192.168.100.0/24, allow BGP from explicit neighbor IPs, accept OSPF protocol traffic, and then log-and-discard all others. A common misconception is that applying filters to physical interfaces alone is sufficient to protect the control plane; without a lo0 input policy, traffic targeting router addresses arriving on different interfaces could still reach the C P U. When designing CPP, include accept terms for needed protocols, explicit source prefixes for management, and an explicit discard term with logging so you can audit what was blocked. Always keep an out-of-band console or rollback plan because strict lo0 policies can block administrative access if misconfigured. How will you balance strictness and recovery options in your CPP policy?

keyIdea.text: An input filter on lo0 centralizes control plane protection for all addresses processed by the router.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Control Plane Protection (CPP)
Why lo0 matters

Packets destined for router IPs are processed by the CPU. A lo0 input filter lets you control which of those packets reach the control plane regardless of ingress interface.

Best practices
  • Permit SSH from specific management prefixes only.
  • Permit BGP only from defined peer IPs and OSPF protocol as necessary.
  • Include a discard with log term to audit blocked attempts.
Safety and testing

Maintain console or out-of-band access and test filters incrementally so you never lock out management during deployment.

Key Takeaway

Use lo0 input filters to centralize control plane defense, permit only necessary sources and protocols, and keep recovery options available.

screens.title: Walkthrough: PROTECT_LO0 filter
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the PROTECT_LO0 example configuration and explain each term. The filter defines specific terms: ALLOW_MGMT_SSH matches TCP from 192.168.100.0/24 to destination port 22 and then accepts; ALLOW_BGP_PEERS matches TCP from explicit neighbor addresses to destination port 179 and accepts; ALLOW_OSPF matches OSPF protocol and accepts. A final DISCARD_ALL_OTHERS term logs and discards anything else. When you commit this filter and then apply it as an input on lo0, only those explicitly permitted packets will reach the router C P U. A common testing strategy is to first permit the management host and check SSH from that host, then test a different source to confirm it is discarded, and finally check show firewall filter PROTECT_LO0 counter to see hits on ALLOW_MGMT_SSH or DISCARD_ALL_OTHERS. If you rely on routing protocols such as BGP and OSPF, be sure to list the correct neighbor IPs and allow the appropriate protocol types. The configuration example below is the exact structure you can use. Remember to have an out-of-band plan prior to committing when adjusting lo0 policies. Walkthrough: PROTECT_LO0 filter means explicit accept terms for management and protocols, then a logged discard, give clear control and auditability for control plane traffic.. In practical terms, step through a real junos configuration for control plane protection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PROTECT_LO0 in practice
keyIdea.text: Explicit accept terms for management and protocols, then a logged discard, give clear control and auditability for control plane traffic.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Walkthrough: PROTECT_LO0 filter
PROTECT_LO0 filter (exact structure)
firewall {
    family inet {
        filter PROTECT_LO0 {
            term ALLOW_MGMT_SSH {
                from {
                    source-address 192.168.100.0/24;
                    protocol tcp;
                    destination-port 22;
                }
                then accept;
            }
            term ALLOW_BGP_PEERS {
                from {
                    source-address 10.0.0.1/32;
                    source-address 10.0.0.2/32;
                    protocol tcp;
                    destination-port 179;
                }
                then accept;
            }
            term ALLOW_OSPF {
                from {
                    protocol ospf;
                }
                then accept;
            }
            term DISCARD_ALL_OTHERS {
                then {
                    log;
                    discard;
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

interfaces {
    lo0 {
        unit 0 {
            family inet {
                filter {
                    input PROTECT_LO0;
                }
                address 192.168.1.1/32;
            }
        }
    }
}
Annotation & test steps
  1. Commit the filter and apply to lo0 as input.
  2. From 192.168.100.x test SSH to the lo0 IP; it should succeed.
  3. From another IP try SSH; it should fail and be logged to messages if log is configured.
  4. Check show firewall filter PROTECT_LO0 counter to see term hits.
Key Takeaway

Explicit accept terms for known sources and protocols, then an explicit logged discard, give control and an audit trail for control plane traffic.

screens.title: Order of operations
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the order of operations helps you predict whether a packet will be dropped or forwarded. In Junos the usual sequence relevant to filters is: first, the input filter is applied as packets arrive on an interface. If the packet is discarded there, processing stops. Next, if uRPF is enabled, the source address is checked to ensure it is reachable via the interface the packet arrived on. If uRPF rejects the packet, it is dropped. After that, the router performs a routing lookup to determine the egress interface and next hop. Finally, any output filter attached to the egress interface is applied before the packet is transmitted. This order has practical implications: an input filter can drop a packet regardless of routing state, while an output filter cannot prevent the router from performing a routing lookup or from spending C P U to process the packet internally. When designing policies, account for uRPF and routing behavior — for example, a source that fails uRPF may be dropped even if an input filter allows it. Verification should check counters and routing state together when behavior seems unexpected. The clear mental model is: input → uRPF → routing lookup → output.

keyIdea.text: Input filter → uRPF → routing lookup → output filter; knowing this order explains many unexpected drops.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Order of operations
Packet processing timeline
1. Input Filter
Applied as packet arrives; can drop early.
2. uRPF
Optional source reachability check on the incoming interface.
3. Routing Lookup
Determines egress interface and next hop.
4. Output Filter
Applied before sending the packet out the egress interface.
Practical implication: if a packet is discarded by an input filter, it never reaches uRPF or routing. If uRPF drops it, you may need to adjust route or interface design rather than the filter. When results are unexpected, check both the filter counters and routing/uRPF state together.
Key Takeaway

Use the processing order to diagnose why a packet was dropped: input check first, then uRPF, then routing, then output.

screens.title: Verifying filters and counters
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is essential after you apply or change a filter. The most direct place to start is show firewall filter counter. This command reports hit counts per term, so you can see whether your explicit accept terms are incrementing or whether packets fall through to an implicit or explicit discard. Next, use show interfaces detail to confirm which filters are applied and in which direction. If you included log actions in a discard term, show log messages will surface those logged events and give packet information you can correlate with counters. For live observation, monitor traffic interface detail captures packets on the interface in real time; include match conditions to narrow results. A useful workflow: apply the filter, use monitor traffic to see whether packets arrive as expected, exercise the traffic from a test host, then check filter counters and logs to confirm the matching term. A frequent discovery is that expected matches don't increment counters because source prefixes or ports are incorrect; comparing captured packet headers to your filter terms usually reveals the mismatch. Always iterate and test incrementally to avoid accidental service disruption.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Verifying filters and counters
Key verification commands
  • show firewall filter <filter-name> counter — term hit counts.
  • show interfaces <interface> detail — which filters are attached and direction.
  • monitor traffic interface <interface> detail — live packet capture.
  • show log messages — see entries from log actions in filter terms.
Workflow

Capture, test traffic from known hosts, then check counters and logs to identify mismatches between packets and filter terms.

Common troubleshooting discovery

If counters for accept terms remain zero while packets arrive, check source prefixes, ports, and protocol matches — often a small mismatch in term criteria is the cause.

Key Takeaway

Measure first. Use counters and captures to locate mismatches, then adjust terms and re-verify incrementally.

screens.title: Monitor traffic and logs
screens.narratorSegment: When counters are inconclusive, a live capture is the next step. monitor traffic interface detail lets you observe packets arriving on an interface with header details such as source and destination IPs, protocol, and ports. Use match conditions to reduce noise and focus on the flow you expect to match a filter term. Compare the captured headers to the term criteria — source-address, protocol, destination-port — to see why a packet did or did not match. If you have log actions in discard terms, show log messages will reveal which term logged the event and provide timestamps you can correlate with captures. A practical approach: start a capture, generate test traffic from your management host, and observe both the capture and filter counter for the target term. If your captured packet shows a different source than you expected, you need to adjust source-prefix-lists or the term's source-address entries. Remember safety: when troubleshooting policies on lo0 or management interfaces, keep a console path available in case a change blocks your remote access. This combined use of monitor traffic, counters, and logs gives you a reliable method to diagnose and correct filtering behavior.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Monitor traffic and logs
Using monitor traffic

Start a capture on the interface you expect traffic to arrive on and include match conditions to reduce noise. Observe headers and timestamps for correlation.

Example command
monitor traffic interface <interface-name> detail
Using logs

If your discard term logs, check show log messages to find entries for dropped packets and the term that logged them. Use timestamps to match against captures.

Troubleshooting tip

If captured packets differ from expected values, adjust source-prefix entries or port matches rather than assuming the router misbehaved.

Key Takeaway

Combine monitor traffic captures and log messages with filter counters to pinpoint why packets are accepted or discarded.

screens.title: Lab: Apply a CPP filter to lo0
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through creating a control plane protection filter for lo0 that allows SSH from a specific management workstation, blocks other TCP destined to the router, and permits other protocols if desired. First, define a prefix-list or prefix set for your management host so the filter can reference a stable object. Next, create the firewall filter with a term that matches the management prefix, protocol tcp, and destination-port 22, then accept it and count hits. Add a term to match other TCP to the router and log and discard it. Optionally add a final accept term for other protocols like OSPF or ICMP if you want to permit them. Apply the filter to lo0 unit 0 family inet using filter input NAME and ensure lo0 has an IP address. Commit the configuration and then verify from the management workstation that SSH succeeds, attempt a second host and validate it fails, and check show firewall filter counter to see the MGMT_SSH_HITS increment. Always have a console or rollback plan before committing. This exercise reinforces the pattern: permit known management, explicitly block undesired TCP, and verify with counters and captures.

keyIdea.title: Practice with safety
keyIdea.text: Define a management prefix, create accept and discard terms, apply to lo0 input, then test and verify with counters.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Lab: Apply a CPP filter to lo0
Step-by-step commands
# 1. Define management host prefix-list
set policy-options prefix-list MGMT_HOSTS {
    192.168.1.100/32;
}

# 2. Define filter terms
set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term ALLOW_MGMT_SSH from source-prefix-list MGMT_HOSTS
set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term ALLOW_MGMT_SSH from protocol tcp
set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term ALLOW_MGMT_SSH from destination-port 22
set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term ALLOW_MGMT_SSH then {
    count MGMT_SSH_HITS;
    accept;
}

set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term BLOCK_OTHER_TCP_TO_ROUTER from protocol tcp
set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term BLOCK_OTHER_TCP_TO_ROUTER then {
    log;
    discard;
}

set firewall family inet filter LO0_PROTECTION term ALLOW_ALL_OTHER_PROTOCOLS then accept

# 3. Apply to lo0
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet filter input LO0_PROTECTION
set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 10.0.0.1/32

# 4. Commit and verify
commit and-quit
show firewall filter LO0_PROTECTION counter
show log messages
monitor traffic interface lo0 detail
Verification

From your management host SSH to the lo0 IP should succeed. From a different IP, SSH should fail. Check counters to confirm.

Safety

Keep a console or out-of-band connection available in case the filter blocks remote management access.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts summarize the most important ideas. First, a firewall filter must be attached to an interface and the correct family before it becomes active — definition alone does nothing. Second, input filters are processed before routing, making them an effective early defense for unwanted ingress traffic. Third, output filters are applied after routing and act as a final check on packets leaving an egress interface. Keep these concepts in mind when designing policies so you apply filters where they will actually control the traffic of interest. When you need to protect the router itself, remember the loopback input pattern described earlier: permit known management and protocol traffic, then log and discard everything else if that is your posture. These ideas help you design predictable, verifiable filter deployments. Key Concepts — Part 1 means attach filters correctly, choose input for early drops, and use output for egress control.. In practical terms, three essential ideas to keep in mind. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Attachment activates filters
A defined filter is inert until bound to an interface and family.
Input runs early
Input filters run before routing decisions and can prevent CPU work.
Output runs late
Output filters are applied after routing lookup as a final egress check.
Summary

In chains, the first terminating match stops later filters; plan order to avoid permissive early matches.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll learn how firewall filters become active only after they are applied, how the application point and direction determine which packets are inspected, and why the loopback interface is the canonical place for control plane protection. You will see concrete examples of input and output filters, the impact of chaining filters, the specific role of lo0 when protecting the router's C P U, and the typical verification commands to confirm behavior. This matters because a misapplied filter can drop legitimate management traffic, lock you out of a device, or fail to stop an attack. For example, allowing SSH only from a management subnet and applying that filter to lo0 lets you restrict who can reach the router itself regardless of the ingress interface. We'll also cover the order of operations — input filter, uRPF checks, routing lookup, then output filter — so you understand when filters drop or allow packets relative to routing decisions. By the end of the lesson you will be able to apply filters to logical interfaces, create a control plane protection policy for lo0, and use Junos verification commands safely. Consider what access you need to preserve before you apply a restrictive filter; that habit prevents accidental lockouts.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply firewall filters to both physical and logical interfaces in Junos OS, choose the correct direction for filtering, and protect the control plane by applying a filter to lo0. You will learn how filters interact with routing and uRPF checks so you can predict when a packet will be accepted or discarded. You will also practice verification and troubleshooting workflows: checking which filters are applied, reading term counters, capturing traffic on an interface, and reviewing logs when log actions are configured. These are practical, testable skills: for example, you will apply an input filter to lo0 that only accepts SSH from a management subnet and then verify hits with show firewall filter counter. You will also be prepared to avoid common mistakes, like applying a restrictive filter to an in-band management interface without a console fallback. Together these objectives give you the procedural and diagnostic skills to apply filters safely and confirm they behave as intended in production.

This second objectives slide focuses on applied skills and safe practices. You will compose filters with explicit terms to accept management protocols like SSH and routing protocols like BGP and OSPF, then place an explicit discard term to log and drop everything else if that is your desired posture. You will learn how to chain filters on the same interface, and why the first terminating action stops later filters in the chain. In a lab exercise you will apply a control plane protection filter to lo0 that accepts SSH from a management host, allows routing protocol traffic, and discards other TCP traffic. You will then test from the management host and from a different IP to observe success and failure. Finally, you'll practice verification using show firewall filter counter and monitor traffic so you can confirm which terms are hit and which packets are falling through to implicit discard. These skills ensure you can enforce policy without accidentally blocking essential services.

A firewall filter in Junos only becomes active when it is applied to an interface and the appropriate family. Defining terms and actions inside the filter does nothing until you bind that filter to a logical unit such as unit 0 and to a family like inet for IPv4. This specificity matters because the same physical interface can support multiple families and logical units; a filter applied to family inet on unit 0 will not affect other families or units. For example, applying a filter to ge-0/0/0.0 family inet ensures IPv4 packets entering or leaving that logical interface are evaluated. A common misconception is assuming a filter defined under firewall will automatically protect interfaces globally — it will not. You must attach the filter to the interface using syntax such as filter input FILTER_NAME under interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet. When you attach a filter, decide whether it should inspect input traffic, output traffic, or both. Attaching to lo0 centralizes protection for packets destined to the router itself. Always verify attachment after commit with show interfaces detail to confirm the filter is present and in the expected direction. The key takeaway is: definition creates capability; attachment makes it operate.

An input filter is applied to packets as they enter the router through a specific interface and is the most common place to enforce security policy. Because input filters are processed before routing lookup, they can stop unwanted traffic from consuming router resources or reaching internal networks. For instance, blocking a malicious SYN flood at the ingress input prevents the router from having to examine or forward those packets. Input filters work at the logical interface and family level — if you want to protect IPv4 arriving on ge-0/0/1, bind a filter under unit 0 family inet and use filter input FILTER_NAME. A common misconception is that an input filter on a single physical interface protects traffic destined to all of the router's IP addresses; it only affects packets arriving on that interface. To centrally protect the router itself, apply a control plane protection filter to lo0. Remember also that input filters are evaluated before unicast reverse path forwarding and routing lookup, so they can drop packets regardless of routing state. A practical check after applying an input filter is to use show firewall filter counter and monitor traffic on the interface to confirm the expected terms are being hit. What packet types will you prioritize in your input policy?

Output filters evaluate packets as they are about to leave an egress interface, after the routing lookup has determined the next hop and egress. Use output filters when you want to control traffic the router sends to a network segment or when you must enforce policy on egress behavior. For example, if you want to prevent the router from sending specific types of traffic to an internal network, applying an output filter on the internal-facing interface ensures those packets are checked after routing. A contrast often confuses students: input filters protect the ingress and can drop packets before the router spends C P U on routing; output filters do not prevent a packet from being routed internally and are applied later in the packet's journey. Another common use is to provide a last layer of defense in a layered policy approach — for instance, accept or rate-limit on ingress, then drop anything undesired before it exits the internal interface. Remember that output filters cannot protect the router's C P U from packets destined for the router itself; for that, use lo0 input filters. Verify output filters the same way with show interfaces detail and show firewall filter counters for the named filter applied outbound, and consider packet captures to confirm filtering behavior.

Junos lets you apply multiple filters in a chain for the same interface and direction, for example input [ FILTER_A FILTER_B ]. When chaining, filters are evaluated in sequence. The first filter that returns a terminating action — accept, discard, or reject — stops further processing. This sequential behavior is important when you design layered policies. For instance, you might place a lightweight, high-performance filter first to drop obvious unwanted traffic, then a more complex filter second for deeper inspection. A common pitfall is placing a permissive accept term too early in the chain so later filters never get an opportunity to apply their tighter rules. Another detail to remember is implicit discard: if no explicit term matches, the packet is discarded by default. That means chained filters must explicitly accept traffic you want to permit or include a permissive final term. When you chain filters, test each filter individually first using counters to ensure it behaves as expected. Use show firewall filter counter for each filter and then apply the chain and re-check to confirm the first-terminating behavior matches your design. How could you order terms to minimize false positives while limiting C P U cost?

Control plane protection uses firewall filters to restrict traffic destined to the router itself — the C P U that processes management and routing protocol packets. The loopback interface, lo0, is the standard place to apply CPP filters because traffic destined to any of the router's IP addresses will ultimately be processed there if lo0 is configured with those addresses. By placing an input filter on lo0 that permits only specific management networks, routing neighbors, and protocol traffic, you centralize protection regardless of the physical interface on which a packet first arrived. For example, a PROTECT_LO0 filter might accept SSH from 192.168.100.0/24, allow BGP from explicit neighbor IPs, accept OSPF protocol traffic, and then log-and-discard all others. A common misconception is that applying filters to physical interfaces alone is sufficient to protect the control plane; without a lo0 input policy, traffic targeting router addresses arriving on different interfaces could still reach the C P U. When designing CPP, include accept terms for needed protocols, explicit source prefixes for management, and an explicit discard term with logging so you can audit what was blocked. Always keep an out-of-band console or rollback plan because strict lo0 policies can block administrative access if misconfigured. How will you balance strictness and recovery options in your CPP policy?

Let's walk through the PROTECT_LO0 example configuration and explain each term. The filter defines specific terms: ALLOW_MGMT_SSH matches TCP from 192.168.100.0/24 to destination port 22 and then accepts; ALLOW_BGP_PEERS matches TCP from explicit neighbor addresses to destination port 179 and accepts; ALLOW_OSPF matches OSPF protocol and accepts. A final DISCARD_ALL_OTHERS term logs and discards anything else. When you commit this filter and then apply it as an input on lo0, only those explicitly permitted packets will reach the router C P U. A common testing strategy is to first permit the management host and check SSH from that host, then test a different source to confirm it is discarded, and finally check show firewall filter PROTECT_LO0 counter to see hits on ALLOW_MGMT_SSH or DISCARD_ALL_OTHERS. If you rely on routing protocols such as BGP and OSPF, be sure to list the correct neighbor IPs and allow the appropriate protocol types. The configuration example below is the exact structure you can use. Remember to have an out-of-band plan prior to committing when adjusting lo0 policies. Walkthrough: PROTECT_LO0 filter means explicit accept terms for management and protocols, then a logged discard, give clear control and auditability for control plane traffic.. In practical terms, step through a real junos configuration for control plane protection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the order of operations helps you predict whether a packet will be dropped or forwarded.
